lead: This unit explains how small molecules join into long chains, how the shape and size of those chains fix the properties of a plastic, and how polymers are measured, made conducting, and combined with fibres into composites. After it you can classify a polymer, write a polymerisation mechanism, compute degree of polymerisation, number and weight average molar mass, and the stiffness of a fibre composite.
about: The unit opens with vocabulary: monomer, repeat unit, degree of polymerisation, and the family tree of polymers (5.1). 5.2 adds tacticity, the three ways side groups can sit along a chain of stereocentres. 5.3 shows how chains are actually made, by chain growth or step growth, and 5.4 gives the Ziegler-Natta route that makes stereoregular chains. With structure in hand, 5.5 connects regularity, branching and cross-linking to crystallinity, strength and softening point. 5.6 lists the addition and condensation polymers you must know by monomer and repeat unit, with rubbers and vulcanisation. 5.7 handles molar mass averages and how light scattering and viscometry measure them. 5.8 turns to conducting polymers, and 5.9 closes with composites, where a polymer or ceramic matrix carries stiff fibres.

chapters.idea: A polymer is a large molecule built by joining many small monomer units, and its class and name follow from that repeat unit.
chapters.depth: Define monomer, repeat unit (some syllabi call it the mer), degree of polymerisation DP, oligomer, homopolymer and copolymer (random, alternating, block, graft). Classify by source (natural, semi-synthetic, synthetic), by heat behaviour (thermoplastic, thermoset, elastomer), by chain shape (linear, branched, cross-linked), and by the number of monomer types. State that functionality must be two or more for a chain to grow. Mention average molar mass only as a name and hand the formulas to 5.7. Keep every definition to one or two lines with an Indian example such as jute, natural rubber or a PET water bottle.

figure.aria: A hierarchy that sorts polymers by three independent questions: where they come from, how they behave on heating, and how their chains are shaped.

chapters.example: A polystyrene sample has molar mass 52,000 g/mol. Its repeat unit is C8H8, molar mass 104 g/mol. Find the degree of polymerisation. Then find the molar mass of a polypropene (C3H6, 42 g/mol) sample with the same DP. Answer: DP = 52,000 ÷ 104 = 500 repeat units. Polypropene with DP 500: 500 × 42 = 21,000 g/mol.
chapters.trap: DP counts repeat units, not carbon atoms. A DP of 500 in polystyrene gives 52,000 g/mol, never 500 g/mol, and the monomer molar mass is not the repeat-unit molar mass when a small molecule leaves.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for covalent bonding and the tetrahedral carbon backbone.
chapters.leave: Mechanisms to 5.3, molar mass averages to 5.7, rubber and vulcanisation detail to 5.6.

chapters.idea: Tacticity is the order in which side groups sit along a chain of stereocentres: all on one side, strictly alternating, or random.
chapters.depth: Start from a vinyl polymer -[CH2-CHX]n- where every second carbon carries X and is a stereocentre. Distinguish configurational isomers (bonds must break to change) from conformations (rotation about single bonds). Define isotactic, syndiotactic and atactic, and give the meso (m) and racemo (r) dyad language some syllabi use, plus mm, mr, rr triads. Note that polyethene has no stereocentre, so tacticity does not apply to it. Say in one line that tacticity controls crystallinity and hand the numbers to 5.5 and the catalyst to 5.4.

figure.aria: A three-branch tree showing the three ideal tacticities of a vinyl polymer chain.

chapters.example: A short vinyl polymer -[CH2-CHX]n- has 5 stereocentres. (a) How many configurational isomers exist if each centre is free? (b) In a fully atactic chain, what dyad and triad fractions are expected? Answer: (a) 2⁵ = 32 isomers. (b) m = r = 0.50, so mm = 0.25, mr + rm = 0.50, rr = 0.25.
chapters.trap: Atactic does not mean no stereocentres; it means the centres exist but their arrangement is random. Isotactic chains also carry no net optical activity in bulk because equal numbers of right and left-handed helices form.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for repeat units; Unit 1 for the tetrahedral carbon.
chapters.leave: How crystallinity changes strength and softening point to 5.5; how catalysts force isotacticity to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Chains are built either by chain growth (addition) with an initiator, or by step growth (condensation) between bifunctional monomers.
chapters.depth: Contrast addition and condensation on three points: whether a small molecule leaves, how molar mass rises with conversion, and which monomers are needed. Then write the free-radical steps: initiation, propagation, termination by combination and by disproportionation, and chain transfer, each with one structural equation. Add cationic, anionic and ring-opening as short paragraphs with one example each. For step growth, require functionality two or more and state that only near complete conversion does DP become large. Keep the kinetics qualitative; rate laws belong to Unit 3.

figure.title: Free-radical chain growth
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from monomer through initiation and propagation to termination, ending in a dead polymer chain.

chapters.example: 1.00 mol of ethene is polymerised with 2.00 mmol of benzoyl peroxide. Each peroxide molecule starts one chain and termination is by disproportionation. Find the number of chains and the number-average DP. Answer: chains = 2.00 × 10⁻³ × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²¹. DP = 6.022 × 10²³ ÷ 1.204 × 10²¹ = 500. If termination were by combination, two radicals form one chain, so DP = 1000.
chapters.trap: Condensation does not always release water (polyurethane releases none), and addition does not always keep the same formula (PVC keeps all atoms, but ring-opening does not). Read the monomer to decide, not the chapter heading.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for monomer and functionality; Unit 3 for rate ideas if a question asks for kinetics.
chapters.leave: Stereocontrol to 5.2 and 5.4; molar mass averages to 5.7; named polymers to 5.6.

chapters.idea: A Ziegler-Natta catalyst is a transition metal compound plus an alkyl aluminium that together insert monomer units in a fixed orientation.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail, so keep it short. Give TiCl4 with Al(C2H5)3, the reduction to solid TiCl3, and the surface site with one vacant coordination position. Describe coordination of the alkene, migration of the growing alkyl chain, and the empty site left behind, which repeats. State that the solid surface forces one orientation, so polypropene comes out largely isotactic, and that this is why HDPE is linear and stiff. Name metallocene catalysts and the Phillips process in one line each.

figure.title: One insertion cycle
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom cycle from catalyst preparation to surface site, alkene binding, chain migration and isotactic polymer.

chapters.example: Catalyst is prepared from TiCl4 (189.7 g/mol) and Al(C2H5)3 (114.2 g/mol) in 1:1 mole ratio. For a batch using 0.050 mol TiCl4, find the mass of each reagent, and the polymer mass if 1.0 kg propene is fed at 85% conversion. Answer: TiCl4 = 0.050 × 189.7 = 9.49 g; Al(C2H5)3 = 0.050 × 114.2 = 5.71 g; polymer = 0.85 × 1.0 kg = 850 g.
chapters.trap: The alkyl aluminium is the activator, not the polymerising centre; the transition metal site does the inserting. Also do not claim Ziegler-Natta gives atactic polypropene, since stereoregularity is its whole point.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for tacticity and 5.3 for chain growth.
chapters.leave: Industrial reactor details and metallocene kinetics outside this unit; 18-electron counting to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Chain regularity, branching, cross-linking and molar mass decide how well chains pack, and packing decides crystallinity, stiffness, density and softening point.
chapters.depth: Go cause to effect in four steps: structure, packing, crystallinity, property. Cover tacticity and chain regularity, branching (LDPE versus HDPE), cross-linking (thermoset and vulcanised rubber), molar mass, and intermolecular forces such as hydrogen bonding in nylon and dipoles in PVC. Define glass transition temperature Tg and melting point Tm and say which polymers are rubbery at room temperature. Give the density formula for mass fraction crystallinity with every symbol defined. Keep elastomer elasticity to one paragraph with the idea of chain uncoiling and recoiling.

figure.title: Two chains, two behaviours
figure.aria: Two parallel chains of cause and effect: a regular linear chain packs into a crystalline stiff solid, while a branched chain packs poorly and stays soft.

chapters.example: A polyethylene sample has density ρ = 0.940 g/cm³. The fully amorphous density is ρa = 0.850 g/cm³ and the fully crystalline density is ρc = 1.000 g/cm³. Find the mass fraction of crystallinity. Answer: fraction = ρc(ρ - ρa) ÷ [ρ(ρc - ρa)] = 1.000 × 0.090 ÷ (0.940 × 0.150) = 0.090 ÷ 0.141 = 0.638, that is 63.8% crystalline.
chapters.trap: Higher crystallinity raises density, stiffness and Tm but lowers transparency and flexibility. A question that says stronger and clearer in one breath is testing this trade-off, not asking for a single trend.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for classification, 5.2 for tacticity, 5.3 for branching routes.
chapters.leave: Molar mass averages to 5.7; named polymer properties to 5.6; fibre reinforcement to 5.9.

chapters.idea: Each important polymer is remembered by its monomer, its repeat unit, whether it is addition or condensation, and one use.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities expect this many names, so use a short list with structure and use. Addition: PE, PP, PVC, PS, PTFE. Condensation: nylon 6,6, nylon 6, PET, polycarbonate, bakelite, urea-formaldehyde. Add natural rubber as cis-polyisoprene, vulcanisation with sulfur cross-links, and synthetic rubbers SBR and nitrile rubber. A few syllabi also add silicon polymers, so give one line on the Si-O-Si backbone of polysiloxanes (silicones) used as oils and sealants. Give one-line uses in Indian context: PVC pipes, PET bottles, tyre rubber.

figure.aria: A two-branch tree grouping six must-know polymers into addition and condensation families with their monomers or uses.

chapters.example: Nylon 6,6 is made from adipic acid (146 g/mol) and hexamethylenediamine (116 g/mol), and two water molecules (18 g/mol each) leave per repeat unit. Find the repeat-unit molar mass and the molar mass of a sample with DP = 100. Answer: repeat unit = 146 + 116 - 36 = 226 g/mol; sample = 226 × 100 = 22,600 g/mol, about 2.26 × 10⁴ g/mol.
chapters.trap: Subtract the small molecule per repeat unit, not per monomer pair only once, and never use monomer molar mass for a chain calculation. PET loses two water molecules per repeat unit, nylon 6,6 also loses two.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 for mechanism types, 5.1 for repeat units.
chapters.leave: Rubber elasticity theory to a polymer course; composite matrices to 5.9; molar mass measurement to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A polymer sample is a mixture of chain lengths, so its molar mass is reported as an average, and the average used must match the method used.
chapters.depth: Define number average Mn, weight average Mw, viscosity average Mv and z average Mz with their summation formulas, each term explained, and define polydispersity index PDI = Mw/Mn. Show why Mn is pulled down by short chains and Mw up by long ones. Cover methods briefly: end-group analysis and osmometry for Mn, light scattering for Mw (say only that scattering intensity grows with Mw and mention the Zimm plot by name), viscometry for Mv through the Mark-Houwink relation [η] = K M^a, and gel permeation chromatography for the whole distribution. Light scattering gets one short paragraph, not a derivation.

figure.aria: Two bell-shaped distributions of chain length; the broad one has the same peak but long tails on both sides, which pull the weight average above the number average.

chapters.example: A sample has 10 g of chains of molar mass 10,000 g/mol and 30 g of chains of molar mass 40,000 g/mol. Find Mn, Mw and PDI. Answer: moles = 10/10,000 + 30/40,000 = 0.0010 + 0.00075 = 0.00175 mol; Mn = 40 g ÷ 0.00175 mol = 22,857 g/mol. Weight fractions are 0.25 and 0.75, so Mw = 0.25 × 10,000 + 0.75 × 40,000 = 2,500 + 30,000 = 32,500 g/mol. PDI = 32,500 ÷ 22,857 = 1.42.
chapters.trap: Light scattering gives Mw, not Mn, and osmometry gives Mn, not Mw. Also check units: molar mass in g/mol, not kg/mol, before quoting a PDI.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for DP and 5.3 for how many chains form.
chapters.leave: Full light-scattering theory to a physics or polymer course; effect of molar mass on strength sits in 5.5.

chapters.idea: A conducting polymer has a backbone of alternating single and double bonds, and chemical doping turns it from an insulator into a conductor.
chapters.depth: Explain conjugation, delocalised pi electrons and the band gap in words, with trans-polyacetylene as the example. Define doping as chemical oxidation (p-type) or reduction (n-type), and describe the polaron and bipolaron as charged defects that carry current along the chain and hop between chains. Give the conductivity range from insulator to near metal, and note that conductivities are quoted in S/cm. Name polyaniline, polypyrrole and PEDOT:PSS with one application each: antistatic coatings, sensors, OLEDs, EMI shielding, supercapacitor electrodes. Mention the four-probe method for measurement and that these films are usually intractable and processed as dispersions.

figure.title: Doping a conjugated chain
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom sequence from a conjugated polyacetylene chain through doping and charged defects to a conducting film.

chapters.example: A doped polyaniline film is 2.0 cm long, 1.0 cm wide and 0.10 cm thick. Its resistance along the length is 40 Ω. Find the conductivity. Answer: area A = 1.0 × 0.10 = 0.10 cm²; σ = l ÷ (R A) = 2.0 ÷ (40 × 0.10) = 0.50 S/cm. Copper is about 10⁵ S/cm, so the film conducts but is far below a metal.
chapters.trap: Doping here is chemical oxidation or reduction of the chain, not adding impurity atoms to a semiconductor lattice. Watch units: S/cm and S/m differ by a factor of 100.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the chain and Unit 6 for band structure of solids.
chapters.leave: Semiconductor doping to Unit 6; battery and supercapacitor device detail to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A composite is two materials kept separate, a matrix that holds and protects and a reinforcement that carries load, so the pair is stronger per kilogram than either alone.
chapters.depth: Define matrix and reinforcement, and why bonding between them matters. Classify into polymer matrix (PMC), ceramic matrix (CMC) and metal matrix (MMC) composites, with fibre, particulate and laminate forms. For PMCs give glass, carbon and aramid fibres in epoxy or polyester, and the processes hand lay-up, pultrusion and resin transfer moulding. For CMCs give SiC-SiC and Al2O3-SiC, made by hot pressing or chemical vapour infiltration, and used where hardness and heat resistance matter, such as brake discs and cutting tools. Give the rule of mixtures with symbols defined, and state its assumption of continuous aligned fibres.

figure.aria: A tree splitting composites by matrix into polymer, ceramic and metal types, with the polymer and ceramic branches expanded into named examples.

chapters.example: A unidirectional glass fibre-epoxy composite has fibre volume fraction Vf = 0.60. Glass fibre modulus Ef = 70 GPa and density 2.5 g/cm³; epoxy modulus Em = 3.5 GPa and density 1.2 g/cm³. Find the composite modulus along the fibres and its density. Answer: Ec = Vf Ef + Vm Em = 0.60 × 70 + 0.40 × 3.5 = 42 + 1.4 = 43.4 GPa. Density = 0.60 × 2.5 + 0.40 × 1.2 = 1.5 + 0.48 = 1.98 g/cm³. Specific modulus = 43.4 ÷ 1.98 = 21.9 GPa per g/cm³, against 2.9 for epoxy alone.
chapters.trap: The rule of mixtures holds for continuous fibres pulled along their length. For short or randomly oriented fibres it overestimates stiffness, and across the fibres the composite is much weaker than the rule predicts.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for matrix properties, 5.6 for epoxy and polyester resins.
chapters.leave: Thin film deposition (PVD, CVD) and nanomaterial synthesis to Unit 6.
